ideal_answer: I choose algorithms based on the problem type, data size, and interpretability requirements. For classification: logistic regression for interpretability, random forests for robustness, XGBoost for tabular data with best performance, and neural networks for complex patterns. For regression: linear regression as a baseline, gradient boosting for non-linear relationships. For clustering: K-Means for known k, DBSCAN for arbitrary shapes and noise. I always start with a simple baseline, then add complexity only when justified by metrics. I understand the assumptions of each algorithm and validate them on my data.

Feature engineering is often the highest-leverage activity in ML. I create features from domain knowledge — for time series data I extract lag features, rolling means, and seasonal components. For text I use TF-IDF, word embeddings, or sentence transformers. For categorical features with high cardinality I use target encoding or embeddings rather than one-hot encoding. I handle skewed distributions with log or Box-Cox transforms. I detect and remove highly correlated features with a correlation matrix. I use mutual information or permutation importance for feature selection to reduce dimensionality and improve generalization.

Statistical thinking is central to data science. I use hypothesis testing to make data-driven decisions — t-tests for comparing means, chi-squared for categorical associations, and Mann-Whitney for non-normal distributions. I understand that p-value is the probability of the data under the null hypothesis, not the probability the hypothesis is true. I avoid p-hacking by setting alpha before the experiment. For A/B tests I calculate required sample size with a power analysis upfront. I use confidence intervals to communicate uncertainty and Bayesian methods when I want to incorporate prior knowledge or update beliefs incrementally.

I use stratified k-fold cross-validation to get robust estimates of generalization performance, especially with imbalanced classes. I separate the test set completely and never touch it until final evaluation to avoid information leakage. For classification I report precision, recall, F1, and ROC-AUC. For imbalanced problems I use PR-AUC which is more informative than ROC-AUC. I check for overfitting by comparing train vs validation learning curves. Calibration is evaluated with reliability diagrams. I use SHAP or LIME for model explainability and to validate that the model is using features for the right reasons.
